Results & Discussion · LOYO-CV Vegetation Forecasting

Reading the LOYO-CV Figures

Figure-by-figure analysis of the Leave-One-Year-Out cross-validation results for 10 forecasting methods across 3 pixels and 11 held-out years (2012–2022), each scored against raw observed LAI.

10 methods (8 AELSTM-family + Chronos-2 zero-shot/LoRA) 3 pixels 11 held-out years, fixed 12-year training window per fold
Overview

Across 330 held-out folds, two forecasting behaviors recur throughout the four figures below: performance is generally strong and stable at pixels with a large, clean seasonal cycle, and it is punctuated by isolated, severe failures at pixels with weaker or noisier seasonal signals. Random Forest and zero-shot Chronos‑2 are the most consistently competitive methods; LoRA fine-tuning is the most volatile; and the two most extreme failures in the study have distinct, physically identifiable causes rather than a shared one.

Figure 1

Distribution of R² across held-out years, per model and pixel

Figure 1 summarizes each method's full year-to-year distribution of forecast skill rather than a single point estimate, making it possible to separate typical-year performance from worst-case behavior. At high_amplitude_deciduous, all ten methods occupy a narrow, high band (R² 0.89–0.99) with substantially overlapping boxes, indicating that method choice has a comparatively small effect at this pixel relative to natural year-to-year variation. At low_amplitude and evergreen, boxes are both lower and wider, and — critically — every method shows exactly one outlier point sitting far below its own whisker, most extreme at evergreen (roughly −4.5 to −8.5).

This single-outlier pattern, repeated identically across all ten methods, is direct visual evidence that poor mean performance at these two pixels is driven by one anomalous year rather than by generally unreliable forecasting. The effect on summary statistics is large: at evergreen, the mean (diamond) sits at or below zero for every method, while the median (line) remains a respectable 0.48–0.68. Reporting the mean alone at either pixel would misrepresent typical-year skill; this is why both statistics are reported throughout this study.

Two comparative observations follow directly from the boxes and outliers. First, at low_amplitude, SVM and zero-shot Chronos‑2 have visibly the narrowest interquartile ranges and the least extreme outliers of the ten methods, suggesting comparatively greater (though not complete) resistance to this pixel's dominant failure mode. Second, at evergreen, the severity of each method's single outlier differs meaningfully — SVM's worst year reaches only R²≈−4.5, markedly less severe than LoRA fine-tuning's ≈−8.5 — despite near-identical median performance (0.48–0.68) across methods in typical years. Method choice therefore has little bearing on typical-year accuracy at this pixel but a substantial bearing on downside risk in an anomalous one.

Figure 2

Ranking frequency across all 33 folds

Figure 2 aggregates relative standing rather than absolute skill, which is necessary because the three pixels operate on very different R² scales (Figure 1) and are not directly comparable in raw terms. Random Forest and zero-shot Chronos‑2 occupy the two lowest mean ranks, each finishing in the top 3 on close to three of every five folds (20/33 and 21/33 respectively) while rarely finishing in the bottom 3 (3 and 6 folds). CNN and AELSTM anchor the opposite end: CNN finishes in the bottom 3 on 19 of 33 folds (58%), and AELSTM on 12 of 33 (36%), with each recording only 2 top-3 finishes across the entire study.

The most notable pattern is the bimodal profile of LoRA fine-tuning. It records 13 top-3 finishes — more than SVM or BiLSTM — but also 15 bottom-3 finishes, second only to CNN, and correspondingly the smallest middle-tier count (5) of any method. This is direct evidence that fine-tuning does not shift Chronos‑2's accuracy uniformly relative to its zero-shot counterpart; instead, it widens the spread of outcomes in both directions. This is consistent with the fine-tuning procedure used in this study running for a fixed number of steps without a validation-based stopping criterion, a design choice that would be expected to increase fold-to-fold variability rather than produce a systematic improvement or decline.

Grouped by modeling paradigm, the two most dependable methods (Random Forest, a tree ensemble; zero-shot Chronos‑2, a pretrained foundation model with no per-pixel training at all) share no architectural lineage, while the two least dependable methods (CNN, AELSTM) are both neural networks trained from scratch on a single pixel's history. Within this study, data efficiency and a well-calibrated prior — whether from ensembling or from large-scale pretraining — appear to matter more for cross-year generalization than architectural capacity trained on a small, pixel-specific dataset.

Figure 3

Year difficulty, standardized within each pixel

Because the three pixels have non-overlapping absolute R² ranges (Figure 1), Figure 3 standardizes difficulty within each pixel before comparing across them. Two cells are sharply distinguished from the rest of the matrix: evergreen/2012 (z=−3.0) and low_amplitude/2018 (z=−2.9), both far exceeding any other deviation. A much milder pattern is visible at high_amplitude_deciduous in 2020 (z=−1.2) and 2021 (z=−1.7), while 2018 at that same pixel is the single easiest fold in the entire study.

No column in the matrix is red across more than one row at a magnitude comparable to the two dominant outliers. Within this three-pixel sample, forecast difficulty is therefore pixel-specific rather than driven by a single event shared across vegetation types — ruling out the simplest explanation for the two extreme cells (a continent-scale climate anomaly affecting all three pixels comparably) and motivating the pixel-specific investigation in Figure 4.

A minor co-occurrence is visible at 2016, where both low_amplitude (z=−0.25) and high_amplitude_deciduous (z=−1.0) show mildly negative values. At this magnitude the pattern does not approach the significance of the two dominant outliers, and this study's three-pixel, eleven-year sample is too small to distinguish a weak shared signal from coincidence; no further claim is made about it here.

Figure 4

Outlier fold investigation: actual LAI vs. training climatology

At evergreen, the actual and climatological curves track closely through the first three months of 2012, then diverge sharply from early April: the climatology continues rising toward its expected seasonal peak of approximately 5.0–5.1 in May–June, while the actual trajectory peaks at only ~3.9 in early April before declining, remaining 1.5–3.5 LAI units below climatology for the rest of the year and closing 2012 near 1.5–1.6, the lowest values in the record. This sustained, months-long suppression of canopy greenness is consistent with the documented 2011–2012 US Southeast drought and constitutes a genuine, physically interpretable climate anomaly rather than a data artifact.

At low_amplitude, the failure mode is qualitatively different. Rather than a sustained divergence in one direction, the actual 2018 trajectory oscillates above and below the climatology roughly every one to two 8-day steps — for example, a drop to 0.13 in late February followed immediately by a rise to 0.28, or a rise to 0.36 in April followed by a fall to 0.20 the next period — and includes a sharp end-of-year dip to 0.10 with no counterpart in the smooth climatological curve. Because this pixel's climatological amplitude spans only about 0.15–0.20 LAI units peak-to-trough, these short-term fluctuations are large relative to the total seasonal signal, so R² collapses even without any sustained directional anomaly.

Together, the two panels show that "outlier fold" is not a single failure mode in this study: evergreen/2012 is a low-frequency, high-amplitude, physically explainable climate event that biases predictions in one direction for months, while low_amplitude/2018 is a high-frequency, small-amplitude departure from an already weak seasonal signal. Every method in this study was trained on climate-driven windows of comparable design and had no mechanism to anticipate either pattern from its own training period, which is why the degradation seen in Figures 1–3 is shared across all ten methods rather than isolated to a single model family.

Synthesis

Read together, the four figures support a consistent account of this cross-validation study. Typical-year skill is high and comparable across methods at the pixel with the strongest seasonal signal (Figure 1), and differences between methods become visible mainly through their behavior in atypical years rather than through everyday accuracy. Random Forest and zero-shot Chronos‑2 are the two methods that combine strong typical-year performance with comparatively contained downside risk (Figures 1–2); LoRA fine-tuning trades consistency for occasional strong results, without a net improvement over zero-shot (Figure 2). The two folds responsible for nearly all of the extreme values in this study are pixel-specific and mechanistically distinct — a sustained drought at one pixel, a noisy non-seasonal year at another (Figures 3–4) — a distinction that would not be visible from any single fixed test year, and is the central methodological justification for evaluating across multiple held-out years rather than one.
